messages.subject: Re: Saddle Point (non-maximum) in the output
messages.body_plain:
This output was only recently introduced on the dev version, and I've
since updated it to something like 'Second-order test: model is a
possible saddle point (non-maximum) or information matrix is too
inaccurate'. My guess is it's the latter issue since the S-EM
algorithm has a tendency to not behave nicely on occasions. The dev
version has help to stabilize this matrix a bit more, but the issue
does still occur from time to time.

If you want a more appropriate check, either use different starting
values to see if your model converges to the same log-likelihood
point, which you can invoke by passing GenRandomPars = TRUE.
Alternatively, update your mirt version (current version is 1.1.10)
and use either the SE.type = 'crossprod', 'BL', or 'Louis' information
matrix estimate since these are more exact computations.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Error estimating fitIndices()
messages.body_plain:
I've updated the development version to provide better accuracy for the M2 in bifactor models (and in general), but I don't think it will solve your issue. The problem is that there are a huge number of first and second-order moments that need to be accounted for, and in your case a dense matrix of size 63371 x 63371 has to be inverted....which is no simple task for any personal computer.

I've added an experimental feature to further collapse the tables based on some work by Cai, L. & Hansen, M. Limited-information goodness-of-fit testing of hierarchical item factor models. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 2013, 66, 245-276, but for some reason it doesn't appear to behave well, and causes non-pd matrices. Pull requests are welcome if someone can hunt down what is going on here, since collapsing cells for graded response models will almost certainly solve this issue.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Number of factors to retain in EFA using mirt()
messages.subject_clean: Number of factors to retain in EFA using mirt()
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Feb 7, 2014 at 10:39 PM, Chua Kuan Yong <chua...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
>
> Sorry, another lame question but requires verification nonetheless. In traditional EFA, the number of factors to retain is usually based on a examination of a scree plot. For EFA, eigenvalues > 0 can be retained.

I assume you mean eigenvalues > 1? If they are 0 they account for no variance.

> Can I apply the same logic here also by examining the SS Loadings (eigenvalues) from the mirt() output?

Yes, and that's one approach to follow. Keep extracting factors until the SS is very small for a factor, or equivalently when the factor loadings are all extremely small with no discernible pattern.

>
> This contrasts the approach that you have outline in your vignette, whereby models are compared using AIC or BIC using the anova() function.

I tend to use information statistics in EFA since it punishes more for extracting too many parameters (and may include additional punishment information about small sample sizes, like the BIC). The idea is that if you extract a factor that has very small slopes across all items then including this additional factor doesn't really improve the model fit, and therefore you are wasting degrees of freedom (and incidentally parameter precision) by including them. You can use the AIC/BIC approach in traditional factor analysis as well when modelling with an ML estimator, though only the BIC seems to be computed in the psych package. AIC is easy to calculate though, you just need the number of parameters estimated and the log-likelihood.

```
require(psych)
N <- Harman74.cor$n.obs
R <- Harman74.cor$cov
ml1 <- fa(R,1, n.obs=N, fm='ml')
ml2 <- fa(R,2, n.obs=N, fm='ml')
ml3 <- fa(R,3, n.obs=N, fm='ml')
ml4 <- fa(R,4, n.obs=N, fm='ml')
ml5 <- fa(R,5, n.obs=N, fm='ml')

c(ml1$BIC, ml2$BIC, ml3$BIC, ml4$BIC, ml5$BIC) #three factors lowest with BIC
summary(ml4)
fa.parallel(Harman74.cor$cov, n.obs=N)
```

Phil

> Eric C

messages.subject: whats the more reasonable way to estimate fscores?
messages.subject_clean: whats the more reasonable way to estimate fscores?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

i want to fix an IRT-model to a representative sample and then estimate fscores for another sample. I see two approaches for that:

1. estimate the model, then passing the new data to fscores with the response-pattern option or

2. estimate the model, fix the item parameter, release the GROUP parameter, reestimate the model with both data sets combined.

However, both fscores correlate very high (.999), but at the lower end there is a considerable difference between both approaches (.15 on the theta scale). Why is there a difference, when the item parameter are the same? which approach is the better one?

Thanks a lot!

messages.subject: Re: whats the more reasonable way to estimate fscores?
messages.subject_clean: whats the more reasonable way to estimate fscores?
messages.body_plain:
Hey Felix,

On Thu, Feb 13, 2014 at 10:47 AM,  <bea...@gmx.de> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
>
> i want to fix an IRT-model to a representative sample and then estimate fscores for another sample. I see two approaches for that:
>
> 1. estimate the model, then passing the new data to fscores with the response-pattern option or

This assumes that the calibration and scoring samples are from the
same population, and therefore have the same 'group' level IRT
properties (same means, variances, and distributions).

>
> 2. estimate the model, fix the item parameter, release the GROUP parameter, reestimate the model with both data sets combined.

I'm not sure I understand this approach too well. A more effective way
to observe the problem would be to estimate the model with a multiple
group approach, and constrain the item parameters across groups so
that they are invariant (no DIF). Then you could freely estimate the
group level parameters in one group, which would be made in reference
to the N(0,1) group.

Combining the datasets into one, while ignoring group membership,
effectively makes the model into a weighted average between the two
groups.

>
> However, both fscores correlate very high (.999), but at the lower end there is a considerable difference between both approaches (.15 on the theta scale). Why is there a difference, when the item parameter are the same? which approach is the better one?

It's possible the latent mean/variance are different for the scored
group, which pulls the estimated latent mean/variance away from
N(0,1). I'm not surprised they correlate highly at all, but the mean
of the scores can be farther away from 0 since the prior used in
certain fscores() methods (like EAP and MAP) take the group level
information into account.

Again, a multiple group approach may be more consistent than 2), but
approach 1) is certainly viable if the samples are truly from the same
population. Cheers.

Phil

> Thanks a lot!

messages.subject: Re: empiricalhist
messages.body_plain:
Hey Felix,

The group level parameters are ignored entirely actually, except of
the first iteration (the latent dist shape starts exactly normal, and
deviates from there). By default they are forced to be a standard
normal, so I would leave it as is.

Really the only relevant input is the number of quadrature you use to
approximate the latent distribution non-parametrically (the default is
quite large at 199). This is true for multipleGroup as well. Hope that
helps.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: x axis in plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Carolina,

Yes you can for most plots, and as of the latest release all internal
plots are handled with the high-end lattice package. To modify the
xlim, simply pass the argument to your plotting function and lattice
will take care of the rest. E.g.,

mod <- mirt(Science, 1)
itemplot(mod, 1)
itemplot(mod, 1, xlim = c(-5,5))

The question is whether you really want to do that or not, since
outside this range the internals are not actually evaluated. Perhaps
building your custom plot manually would make sense? There are a good
number of lower level tools available for doing this, like
probtrace(), iteminfo(), expected.item(), etc.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
I don't know too much literature on the topic off the top of my head,
though following the work by Carol Woods would probably be a good
start since she's written a bit about empirical histograms and how
they compare to the splines approach. I'm not entirely convinced our
implementations are the same, but it's a start, and her articles
should provide good references. http://people.ku.edu/~c227w941/

Phil

thanks for providing some input. i played a bit now and estimated a unidimensional, multiple-group grm with empirical histogram approach and i get kind of a wired, right-skewed distribution at theta = 3.9 - 4.0. similar models (e.g. gpcm with emphist, grm without emphist) show a more reasonable distribution of scores (e.g. normal around 2). when i tried to put together a minimal example, the distribution was more reasonable. so i thought, estimation fails at some point and tried different seeds, but i cannot really track down the problem. do you have an idea what happens and how to prevent it?

best wishes, felix
